title: Blair Supports Minister Whose Son Sold Hash To Reporter As Another Calls for Legalization

content_html_sanitized:
LONDON

Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair were embarrassed Wednesday when the 17-year-old son of an unnamed cabinet minister was arrested for selling hashish to a reporter for the Daily Mirror in a London pub. The reporter said she went to the pub after a tip-off and then paid $16.70 for a small packet of hashish, which is the form in which cannabis is most commonly used in Europe.

The newspaper then told the minister, who confronted the son and went with him to a police station Monday where he was arrested and then released on bail. In keeping with the sensationalism of the British press The Mirror -- a pro-Blair paper -- ran the story on five pages. Blair -- a Clinton clone -- has followed an ultra-hard line on drugs, denouncing a campaign by the Independent on Sunday newspaper to have cannabis legalized as "irresponsible."

Blair's official spokesman told reporters: "The prime minister has spoken to the cabinet minister concerned and fully supports the parent's action." The statement appeared to leave open the possibility that the minister involved might have to quit. The boy was not named since defendants under 18 remain anonymous until formally charged. British law allows for a maximum sentence of 14 years jail for selling cannabis but offenders are normally fined if the quantity is small.

Following this incident, the Labour MP, and vice-chairman of the All-party Drugs Misuse Group, Paul Flynn, has called for the recreational use of cannabis to be legalised. Saying, "If the story is true it might help melt the permafrost of prejudice and ignorance of Government policy on recreational drug use. Will they now realise that soft illegal drugs are the non-addictive drugs of choice of most young people - even the middle class children of MPs.The truth is that 50% of young women and 70% of young men between the ages of 20 and 24 in the UK have used illegal drugs. The war is lost. The only way to reduce drug use and drug crime is to collapse the illegal drugs market by replacing it with a legal market that can be policed, regulated and
controlled."

This still seems unlikely as The Home Secretary, Jack Straw, has repeatedly said that the Government does not intend to change the law in relation to cannabis.
